title: Christmas memories of the past... (an epic epistle) | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "roxanna-gw", "author_name": "roxanna", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/roxanna-gw", "date": "2024-11-01", "text": "Time:  the 1950s.  Setting: New England.  Characters: family of 7, five kids + a beloved Heinz57 dog (which ranged free). My dad, altho an MIT graduate in mechanical engineering, never made a big salary.  Our somewhat large family learned early to be frugal and dad's oft-repeated phrase was \"waste not, want not\".  We didn't get everything we wished for by any stretch, and hand-me-downs were ubiquitous, but we didn't feel any lack.  Mum was an excellent cook and taught four daughters to become the same.  Baking was weekly and always, always from scratch.  We all had chores, 10 acres to roam in, and I was 9 years old before we ever had a tv (black&white, of course -- with those old-fashioned tubes that caused the repair fellow to be called for a house call to fix, while we kids sat on the floor and watched him do his magic. Christmas was a fantastic time, which didn't begin in any fashion until Thanksgiving was well past.  Back then, schools were allowed to celebrate with pictures to color, paper snowflakes to be cut, and a definite build-up of anticipation as the big day grew closer. At home, we wriggled with excitement on the day that my mother took us up the attic stairs where she opened the antique dough-box on legs where the tree ornaments resided.  Some had been HER mother's, dating back many decades (I still have a few of these).  Lovely old favorites emerged, to be greeted with joy.  Down the stairs again to the living room, to await the tree.  We never purchased a tree -- either dad or my brother and I cut one from our back forty.  One year, we kids couldn't agree on which tree was better, so we cut two.  My brother's choice was a white pine, which makes a lousy Christmas tree on many levels -- needles too weak and soft to support anything, even the old lead tinsel of those days, and the sap was a terrible thing... The tree was put up only a few days before The Day, and dad secured it in a large base that had four colored light bulbs to increase the festive atmosphere (truly hideous but we kids thought it wonderful).  Then the decorating began!  Nothing fancy or elegant, but we thought it just perfect, naturally.  My personal favorite task was to oh-so-carefully separate the strands of that wonderful lead tinsel into single pieces, as lengthy as I could make them, and smother the entire tree in a veil of silver.  I do still miss that, and haven't done tinsel for decades (altho I actually have two unused boxes of the stuff from the 1950s.  Maybe some day...). The night before, my mother gathered the stockings for Santa to fill and laid them out on each bed.  These were odd stockings that had belonged to ancestors (our family never threw things out, going back generations).  These were the long, well over the knee and we kids loved them, as there was so much room for Santa to fill up!  None of them matched one another, which makes me realize that orphaned single socks are not a modern occurrence -- folk have been dealing with that for eons, clearly! It was such fun to wake before dawn on Christmas morning and search in the darkness for the filled stocking at the foot of our beds, all lumpy in the most intriguing way.  We were not allowed to open them until we carried them into my parent's bedroom, jumped on the bed and then tore into the wonderful treasures.  Always the ubiquitous tangerine or orange at the very toe, and always a new box of Crayola crayons & a new coloring book sticking out of the top. Santa never wrapped his gifts, they all appeared by magic on Christmas morning around the tree, and each of us could tell which was ours, as Santa had cleverly made it apparent by the nature of the gifts.  A stack of books was always my favorite thing to find. Meanwhile, during all the turmoil of gleeful gift examinations, my mother was getting a festive breakfast ready, and dealing with the preparations for the later feast.  Days and even weeks prior to the big day had been spent in baking dozens of cookies, kept on a shelf in huge glass jars, and several pies, polishing the silver, secretly wrapping the family presents and all the other necessary preparations. Everything traditional, beloved and recalled forever.", "images": []}

Describe digital model production. Often referred to as 3D modeling, digital model generation is the creation of three-dimensional object representations using specialist software. This technique can involve creating complex designs from scratch or building models from fundamental geometric forms. Among several sectors, like architecture, product design, automotive, and video gaming, 3D modeling finds great application. Digital modeling streamlines product development in furniture manufacture and offers striking 3D representations for use in marketing brochures, catalogs, and websites. The Forms of Three-D Models Digital models can be created using solid, surface, and wireframe modeling among numerous techniques. Using fundamental geometric forms like spheres and cubes, solid modeling emphasizes building new digital objects. An sophisticated method is surface modeling, in which complicated forms are created via interweaving of curves. Building forms from polygons\u2014small triangles or squares defining the outline of the object\u2014is known as wireframe modeling. High-poly and low-poly models are differentiated between by 3D artists. Ideal for furniture presentations, high-poly models have more polygons, which produces smoother and more photorealistic looks. Low-poly models, on the other hand, are lighter and excel in applications and video games. The Digital Model Manufacturing Methodology The path to produce a 3D model starts with the marketing team giving the 3D studio a brief. As I pass through my incarnations in every age and race,I make my proper prostrations to the Gods of the Market Place.Peering through reverent fingers I watch them flourish and fall,And the Gods of the Copybook Headings, I notice, outlast them all. We were living in trees when they met us. They showed us each in turnThat Water would certainly wet us, as Fire would certainly burn:But we found them lacking in Uplift, Vision and Breadth of Mind,So we left them to teach the Gorillas while we followed the March of Mankind. We moved as the Spirit listed. They never altered their pace,Being neither cloud nor wind-borne like the Gods of the Market Place,But they always caught up with our progress, and presently word would comeThat a tribe had been wiped off its icefield, or the lights had gone out in Rome. With the Hopes that our World is built on they were utterly out of touch,They denied that the Moon was Stilton; they denied she was even Dutch;They denied that Wishes were Horses; they denied that a Pig had Wings;So we worshipped the Gods of the Market Who promised these beautiful things. When the Cambrian measures were forming, They promised perpetual peace.They swore, if we gave them our weapons, that the wars of the tribes would cease.But when we disarmed They sold us and delivered us bound to our foe,And the Gods of the Copybook Headings said: \u201cStick to the Devil you know.\u201d On the first Feminian Sandstones we were promised the Fuller Life(Which started by loving our neighbour and ended by loving his wife)Till our women had no more children and the men lost reason and faith,And the Gods of the Copybook Headings said: \u201cThe Wages of Sin is Death.\u201d In the Carboniferous Epoch we were promised abundance for all,By robbing selected Peter to pay for collective Paul;But, though we had plenty of money, there was nothing our money could buy,And the Gods of the Copybook Headings said: \u201cIf you don\u2019t work you die.\u201d Then the Gods of the Market tumbled, and their smooth-tongued wizards withdrewAnd the hearts of the meanest were humbled and began to believe it was trueThat All is not Gold that Glitters, and Two and Two make FourAnd the Gods of the Copybook Headings limped up to explain it once more. title: Anyone here really commit to a small house as "forever home"? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "adkhiker", "author_name": "adkhiker", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/adkhiker", "date": "2024-11-02", "text": "As my daughter approached age 5, I told my husband this: before she goes into kindergarten, I think we should decide: are we really leaning into this house (1400 sq) and making it work for us, or are we going to move to a bigger house? Because I don't want our daughter to grow up with a house that is constantly in a state of disruption. But, I also don't want to be moving much because of how chaotic that can be. Now, of course, if something major happened, like if my husband lost his highly specialized job in this area, we'd move if we had to. But we have build a beautiful community of people around us over 15 years here - we love our daughter's school (an outdoor private school we can really only afford BECAUSE we live in a smaller home), we have awesome neighbors (the woman on the right of our house is a firefighter, and their son is two - I give them all of our fun toy hand-me-downs.) Our backyard is small but private, and I often wake up to deer grazing on the hill 50 feet from our house and I watch them while I drink my morning coffee. Honestly, I am happy here.What I am not happy with is the amount of work still to be done to the house. For anyone following, we are currently wrapping up the financing for a total kitchen gut. It's exciting, but it's an expensive proposition. Because of the lead paint and asbestos in our 1940s house, we need to pay top dollar to have it safely removed during the renovation. There are so many other projects also on the list: refinishing our main staircase, refinishing the wood floors upstairs, refinishing the flaking basement walls, residing the house, replacing the windows with popped seals, repaving the driveway...I know some of this comes down to just homeownership, you know? After a while we'd incur these costs anywhere. But with labor and materials prices as they are, and with my desire to lean in and make this home our forever home, with quality materials - is it financially stupid? Our kitchen is likely to run us $80k all told. In a house we paid $130k for 15 years ago.I have dreamed since the day we got the keys that we would help this house reach its full potential - turn it into a little jewel box full of charm and warmth.But that was before we had a kid who will, presumably, want to go to college someday. Yes, we are saving for that, too. And retirement. But is it foolish to put so much time and money into a small house?Just random musings on a Saturday morning while I sip my coffee and watch the deer.", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "darbuka", "author_name": "darbuka", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/darbuka", "date": "2024-11-03", "text": "Danger re: quartz (engineered) counters Already banned in Austraila. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-875978293", "author_name": "Nancy Karr", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-875978293", "date": "2024-11-04", "text": "As an MD who has worked with autoimmune diseases including silicosis for decades, and finally getting my kitchen remodel, here are my two cents. Silicosis lung disease has been a proven problem since 1930's when it was shown to be a bigger problem than coal for coal miners disease.  It is a problem for miners, stone cutters, potters, people with hobbies of stone cutting.  The risk is worse with \"confounding factors\" such as smoking, and is a problem with the dust, and proven to be lower risk with decreasing the dust. The amount of silocosis lung disease is much higher since using manufactured stone, and there is no increase in the disease with stone cutters of true stone.  One very high probability is there is a \"confounding factor\" in the mix for making the manufactured stone.  Which of the factors could it be?  We won't know until the companies who make the stone can show that at least one of the other factors is the confounding culprit, and then not use that, not just decreasing the amount of silica crystals.  And I doubt that they will do that, just say oh, look, we have less silica than prior.  Because of this, the ban sounds reasonable until the companies can show the risk goes down to baseline. Fabricators should know and decrease the risk of silica dust, or they are incompetent or they are exploitative or they are risking only themselves in a one person shop. 1.  Use only a fabrication shop that does have ways to decrease the dust exposure, such as water baths, water to decrease the dust and keep their blades sharper.  Ours had no dust in the building and water on the floor from all the water they used, water baths, and the bid was comparable to 3 others in our area and had excellent reviews.  Check out the building, ask what they use to decrease dust.  Silicosis lung disease is awful and progressive and crippling until it is lethal or a person becomes a lung transplant candidate or heart lung candidate if the lung disease damages the heart also.  Its a young persons disease, causing a young, formerly healthy working person to be severely disabled. 2.  The risk of manufactured stone having a confounding factor increasing the risk of silicosis is high, and we do not yet know what that factor may be. 3.  Where did good old Corian go?  My first choice would have been a cream colored Corian with no fake stone look, but it was not made anymore.  Fake stone looks like fake stone to me, whether it is formica or Corian or Quartz.  (We chose quartzite LeBlon)", "images": []}}

I have always found Rhizopon green to be an absolute benefit and use it for all my cuttings...even the incredibly easy salvias and penstemons. title: Solo Japan - A Brief Recap | Houzz Forum

I've tried to understand the difficulty and came to the conculsion that this is a destination trip - meaning it's not next to something where you can drop back in when you visit X.  You purposely come here and stay here.  And there is so darn much you want to see, so it's easy to become overwhelmed.  In fact, three weeks before I was leaving, and after a benign conversation with a client - I changed my itineary! Itineary: Tokyo 7 nights, one day trip to Kamakura Kanazawa 3 nights, one day trip to Takayama and Shirakawago Kyoto 3 nights, no day trips What I did: I saw museums (there was a Monet exhibit in Tokyo, but mostly native Japanese museums), gardens, LOTS of \"city\", shrines, UNESCO sites, nature and 8-10 miles of walking daily What I didn't do: most of the \"tourist\" stuff related to pop culture, \"experiences\", theme parks What I ate: mostly raw fish, rice and snacks!  I ate a number of different things that were mostly very well done, but it was very hot (rain or shine) and I missed out on things like ramen. Another incredible spot I ate at was in the basement of Takashimaya in Kyoto!  Who knew!   Shopping:  This was interesting.  I love vintage designer and follow a number of sellers on the interwebz.  Japan has very strict laws on counterfiet goods.  I have two things to say about that.  First- it's a math problem.  If you divide the volume of pristine resale vintage goods by the population of Japan, I don't see how the math works out.  Second, I personally saw super fake Prada, Chanel and Hermes.  Adding #3....it wasn't in my budget anyways!!!  I did go to an antique fair and bought two kimono and a fully beaded bag for something like $50.  Oh, and an Issay Miyake Bao Bao bag. The only thing I need to figure out is dinner - not that I don't enjoy dining by myself, but I'm going so long during the day - and tend to eat a later lunch - that I just grab snacks and take them back to the room. Kanazawa was both my first area of interest and also my last minute change from Osaka.  It was spetacular.  Beautiful, FRESH fresh fish, less busy and a charming city to walk.  If I had it to do over again, I might see Takayama only.  But the challenge with UNESCO sites here - as with so many places - is that they are absolutely packed with tourists and trinket shops. title: Air handler is not increasing blower speed - no heat | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "huxleys", "author_name": "huxleys", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/huxleys", "date": "2024-11-04", "text": "My upstairs air handler (Lennox Signature CBX32MV) is not increasing the blower speed when the thermostat calls for heat. I have two air handlers fed by hot water from an oil furnace that also provides hot water. The downstairs air handler and hot water are fine and the upstairs was fine until a week ago (further down I have a possible intervening issue) When heat is called upstairs, I hear the coil filling with water (and the circulator pump next to the oil furnace is working). The blower fan starts and runs at what I believe is 490 cubic feet/minute - a very gentle air flow (A-490 is from the air handler's circuit board's 7 segment LED). After several minutes I get an error message on the Lennox Harmony III Zone Control of 'Insufficient Heating' (0101). When I test the blower in idle mode using the built in test on the circuit board in the air handler, I get over 2000 cubic feet a minute. Nor error messages (thus far) on this circuit board. Configurations are correct matching board with unit. I am thinking the sensor is not identifying the increase in heat as air passes over it from the coil as the latter gets hotter. Therefore it doesn't call for the blower to increase speed. But....... The sensor was recently replaced (within last two years). And the system was working fine a week ago. Last Tuesday I had the annual check-up of the oil furnace done. After the technician left, we had no heat - either upstairs or downstairs - and no hot water. They came back two more times and still didn't fix the issue until a third return this past Saturday identified the electrodes to be too high. They also replaced a sensor in the combustion unit and told me the expansion tank was shot. Since then hot water and downstairs heat has been fine. Could the continual call for heat from upstairs, when the boiler wasn't firing, have done something? Is it too much of a coincidence for it to have been working then not working after the service call (but coincidences happen!). Or is it a faulty temperature sensor downstream of the coil? title: What’s with all these mushrooms? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "trainee", "author_name": "KW PNW Z8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/trainee", "date": "2024-11-09", "text": "I asked this question here a few years ago & was told all is fine but I need to ask again.  Why are sooo many white mushrooms popping up in my back yard? As you see from last pic, it\u2019s a long & fairly deep planting bed filled with shrubs, maples, grasses etc. The area is watered by drip irrigation & receives half day of full afternoon sun. This area faces West & is shaded from morning sun by fence & huge firs in property behind.   I have been pulling up the shrooms since I don\u2019t want my dog nibbling on them.  They pop up along at least a 20\u2019 stretch, the largest are overe 6\u201d across, the smaller look like white button mushrooms.  The 2 paniculata hydrangeas are the only thing that gets direct fertilzer.  I have mulched around them but not much else. I know mushrooms spread by spores & thought pulling would eliminate them. This year has been a huge crop. The pics are ones I saw today in 3 separate spots.  Are they good, bad, or indifferent as far as health of my planting bed?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/16525932072eab8d_1824-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/24526171072eab8f_1828-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/4e3242e5072eab92_1831-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a9f273fa072eab95_1833-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: Whole house painting - help! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "simon-grech41", "author_name": "Simon Grech", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/simon-grech41", "date": "2024-11-09", "text": "Our house in the process of being renovated and is going to require painting throughout including the kitchen and bathroom.  We are on a tight budget as we are already spending more than anticipated.  We require a good quality paint though.  The few people I spoke to suggested a dulux paint but wondering whether they are any good quality alternatives.  Also should we buy specialist paint for the bathroom/kitchen? other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jonathandb1972", "author_name": "Jonathan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jonathandb1972", "date": "2024-11-10", "text": "I\u2019m my opinion brands like Dulux make two qualities of paint and the trade paint is better.   So rather than go to the DIY store go to a specialist paint centre and ask them for discount since you will be doing the whole house.    I like Johnson\u2019s and often get them to mix paint for me.   When I was younger (before the days I paid a decorator to do my painting) I didn\u2019t mind using Farrow and Ball paint but most professionals don\u2019t like it.    The message being don\u2019t buy cheap and the professionals don\u2019t like the most expensive paint either. Tips from when i decorated a whole house:Behave like a professional decorator and expect to spend half of your time on preparation work.  Filling and sanding walls can make a huge difference to the end result.When sanding woodwork the goal is to add a key for the new paint not to strip all the old paint- concentrate on rough and chipped areas vacuum and wipe away all dust before painting.If your woodwork is in bad condition then replacing it may not be as expensive as the time spent trying to make it look good.Have common colours that you use again and again to reduce wastage and make it easier to move from room to room.Always paint ceilings first, then walls, then woodwork.Always cut in first and do it twice before turning to a roller.Keeping your roller covered in paint until the next day doesn\u2019t work as dried paint on the roller leaves a bad finish, furthermore washing the roller is tedious.  Since rollering is the quickest part of decorating consider rollering several rooms one after another to avoid repeatedly washing your roller.Choose a Matt finish paint- low light reflectivity disguises imperfections where high sheen highlights im detect walls or application.Brilliant white is rarely the easiest colour to live with- my preference is ceilings and woodwork in a softer white.Don\u2019t be tempted to paint everywhere white, it\u2019s not easier it just means you are postponing putting a colour on the walls.Don\u2019t paint everywhere grey- it\u2019s not modern it\u2019s boring and cold.Websites like Farrow and ball are brilliant for helping you understand colours as ever colour is explained so it\u2019s easy to find a neutral that is stone/beige or includes a green undertone to compliment the sofa. Choose two neutral colours for your walls, one pale and one mid toned- when choosing your neutral think about what you have to work with- for instance if you have inherited a beige carpet or have green sofa then you know what colours you need.Use these neutrals again and again for a cohesive look. Don\u2019t stress that you have made the wrong decisions because you can\u2019t tell until curtains are up and the room is full of furniture. Don\u2019t stress about the colour because you can\u2019t go wrong with neutrals and when you are finished you can reserve the right to paint one wall a stronger colour or to add wallpaper knowing that changing the colour of one wall will take no time if the prep was previously completed and the ceiling and woodwork are already done.", "images": []}}

Zinnias, despite a bad case of mildew this year, finally petered out just last week, although I left a few with buds on them out there.  Some cosmos plants still pumping out blooms and buds too. Marigolds and salvia are still going strong, and my annual pots are still looking fairly good too. I usually put down my shredded leaf mulch at the end of November, beginning of December (although the last few years it has been being put off till late December due to warming conditions) after the ground freezes, and we are probably nowhere near that mark. The question I have is where to prune. If I simply deadhead, I am left with pairs of buds all along the stem (like the attached photo) and if we have another mild winter I will have lots and lots of flowers in small stems when I would rather have fewer flowers on long stems. The problem with buds is that it is hard to tell if they are leaf-only buds or flower buds. Consider also moving the shrub to another location where it can grow as needed without having to require frequent pruning; in its place, plant a more compact hydrangea macrophylla that maybe gets 3 feet high/wide only and reblooms: Summer Crush, Pop Star, selected few from the Let's Dance Series, etc. Nice dark stems in the picture. General Notes:  We do not have a garage, so the kitchen is our only space for a fridge unless and until we build the outdoor kitchen. Engineered hardwood comes in two  different types of cores, one is a plywood core, which has traditionally  been used to make engineered hardwood and the other is newer option  known as high density fiberboard (HDF) core. Even though, it would seem  that a plywood core would be the better choice, the HDF core is harder,  more stable and more moisture resistant, due to its Janka hardness  rating of 1700. In comparison, traditional plywood core is made from  hardwood species with a lower Janka hardness rating as low as 500 for  Poplar or as high as 1200 for Birch. The core is the foundation for the  hardwood so, the higher the Janka hardness rating is for the core, the  harder it will be and will offer more support to the hardwood flooring,  making it more firm and dent resistant. \" The plywood core is constructed by gluing and compressing layers of  thin wood together in a crisscross pattern. The high density fiberboard  core is made from recycled hardwood, which is manufactured by grinding  damaged or defective hardwood into a sawdust and mixing it with a resin,  then, compressing it together to form HDF core. This makes the much HDF  core much harder, more durable and less susceptible to moisture than a  plywood core. For this reason, the HDF core is recommended for areas  with high humidity, drastic climate changes or near bodies of water.\" \"", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2024-11-17", "text": "Ficus shed foliage for a number of reasons. Moving a tree from a bright spot to a dimmer location can cause a shift in the flow of a growth regulator (auxin), which often triggers leaf loss. A real deficiency of any nutrient considered mobile in the plant (nitrogen, phosphorous, potassium, magnesium) or a culturally induced (antagonistic) deficiency can also cause shedding. How should I move forward with this ficus?", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2024-11-18", "text": "If you are monitoring moisture levels with a wooden \"tell\", you're probably doing well insofar as watering intervals are concerned. If your tree can go more than a week between waterings, the grow medium is probably holding too much water to achieve best results. There are a couple of ways to help alleviate that issue if it proves to be a problem, so let me know how long your watering intervals are so we can correct if required. A healthy root system is an absolute prerequisite to a healthy plant, and you simply cannot have the later w/o the former. You should be able to water a planting to beyond the point of saturation, at will, without having to worry that your soil will remain waterlogged so long that excess water in the soil will deprive the root system of oxygen, and in doing so limit normal root function and/or negatively impact root health. Water uptake (and therefore nutrient uptake) is an energy-driven process that must take place in the presence of oxygen, an element essential to the 'burning' of the plant's food (sugar/ glucose) that produces energy for roots' metabolic functions. Ideally, you would be using a grow medium that passively allows enough water to drain from soils that you needn't worry about root function/health issues. If it doesn't happen passively, there are ways to take an active role, which I alluded to above. Water so you're flushing the soil with each watering. Water slowly so you're certain the entire soil column is saturated and at least 20% of the total volume of water used exits the drain hole. Do not allow to rest in water that exits the drain as the practice eliminates the benefit of flushing accumulating solids (salts) from tap water and fertilizer solutions from the soil. If you're flushing the soil when you water, fertilize about every 4th watering with a production level dose of Foliage-Pro 9-3-6. Keep track of how many times you have watered by dropping a marble, button, bottle cap, .... on top of the soil after each watering. He only ever slept for about 4 hours a night and seemed super-human in some other aspects of his life. He had this extreme type A energy level and worked long shifts as an MD while single handedly running another business and never needed a list to remember anything. He would scoff if I had to write a list to go to the grocery store. If he ever had down time, he would walk and would often cover many miles a day. He almost never got sick (he never had a cold in his entire life). I'd always been told that people could not function for long periods of time with less than 6 hours of sleep a night. Lo and behold, in 2019 they discovered a genetic mutation that leads to a syndrome that's been named Short Sleep Syndrome. Other characteristics of the syndrome include Type A personality  (being extremely driven and active), having an outgoing personality, and the ability to memorize lots of info. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2024-11-18", "text": "^^ I think it's much worse than that. There is water on the top sash, but there's a lot of water on the floor and we see it wicked into the OSB wall siding above the plate and wicked into the stud sitting on top of the plate. There's already mold forming on the plate. That's a lot of water being funneled into the wall behind the wrap. Even an un-taped window properly installed would not leak THAT badly. You would cut back a flap at the top and pin it up before installing the window. Then a piece of wrap at top that wraps over the header and overlaps the sides. The sides and bottom wrap around to the inside of the opening and the opening gets caulked before placing the window. Then the top flap that was pinned up comes down over and then things get taped. The shingled layering of the wrap such that water is directed out and away from the building is the primary water proofing. Caulk under the window and tape on seams makes it nice and tight, but are no substitute for properly layered wrap. I just can't imagine THAT amount of water if things were layered properly. The bedroom would be a flex room/play room so kids and I can see each other when I'm in the kitchen. Doors would keep it a legal bedroom that I can use as a guest room on occasion. title: On the obsession with perfection.... | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "diana-bier-interiors-llc-pfvwus-pf~125880644", "author_name": "Diana Bier Interiors, LLC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/interior-designers-and-decorators/diana-bier-interiors-llc-pfvwus-pf~125880644", "date": "2024-11-19", "text": "In a powder room that was renovated a few years back, I just happened to notice that the switchplate is slightly askew, not perfectly placed.  My contractor is fabulous, his work is top quality, but in this one little instance, not perfect.  The electrician was probably tired and wanted to get home to a glass of beer and a hot meal.  Not a big deal. It got me thinking about a lot of design dilemmas I read that go \"what is the perfect white/gray/beige, etc. color for my kitchen/bath/living room?\"  or \"Does this end table go with the bed?\" or \"Can I use a stripe with this check?\" or \"Marble is out--I couldn't deal with the etching/chipping/high maintenance\" or \"I'm doing a kitchen with white cabinets, a beige floor, taupe counter tops and off-white backsplash, because all neutrals go together,\" and the worst \"will this be dated in 5 years?\" When did we all get so obsessed with everything being perfect?  The stress level is sky-high, and renders many of us in analysis/paralysis, unable to make any decisions, losing sleep, \"struggling\" with where to place some wall decor, pulling our hair out in the quest for perfection.  And of course perfection for the next unknown owner in the event of \"resale.\" And then I see a home in the UK, with a fantastically jumbled array of textiles, a riot of color, not much \"matches.\"  The old stone floor chipped and worn, the grout flaking.  Books are piled up on tables, under tables, on chairs.  Curtain rods not quite level, and it is written that the panels are from a grandmother who had them in a chest for 30 years.  Warm, welcoming, a place where everyone feels at home.  No one notices the ring marks on the tables, the scratches on the hardwood floors, or the frayed ends of the skirt on the sofa.  They just know that they will have a memorable time here. Who started this craziness?  I just watched the Netflix special on Martha Stewart, and she is a self-described perfectionist.  Picture perfect food and homes.  All done (at first) by herself, but at the expense of her relationship with husband and daughter.  And like sheep, everyone wanted to have a \"Martha\" home.  The home shows on HGTV are also part of the problem.  Huge renovations done on a budget in a week, and oh-so-perfect.  Not.  Thank you Joanna, Christina, and those hunky twins (I forget their names). I get it that renovations cost money, and no one wants to make costly mistakes.  But I think we need to start easing up.  Do your research and in the end do what you want.  What you like.  If you like it now, you'll probably like it in 20 years.  It won't ever be perfect, so maybe settle for \"good enough\" and enjoy living.", "images": []}

title: Tart talk (not “tarts talking”) | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "mtnrdredux-gw", "author_name": "mtnrdredux_gw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mtnrdredux-gw", "date": "2024-11-19", "text": "I have recently been watching Ina Garten\u2019s Be My Guest. I decided to make her French Apple Tart she demonstrated on the show. It may be a good choice for some of you at Thanksgiving.? https://barefootcontessa.com/recipes/french-apple-tart   The tart depends on a thin crust and very thin apples, which are supposed to caramelize as they bake, due to copious amounts of sugar sprinkled on top. I divided the ingredients in half to make a Test Tart. For my first try, the crust burned badly at the edges and the apples did not caramelize. The latter was probably because I could not bear sprinkling the tart with that much sugar. The former was the whim of the oven gods. For Tart Redux, I sliced the apples more thinly (using a mandoline), caved on the sugar, lowered the temp 25F and kept it in 45min in instead of 40min the first time. It was better, but not perfect. At least it looked more like hers:   There is a tension between caramelizing and browning the apples, and not burning the crust. The recipe even says \u201cDon\u2019t worry! The apple juices will burn in the pan but the tart will be fine!\u201d Well, not exactly. The juices that burn in the pan also seep under the tart, burning some of the underside of the crust. What about that, Ina? The tart is finished with a glaze made from apricot preserves and Calvados. I didn\u2019t bother doing that with (failed) Tart 1 but I did with Tart Redux, and I think that is really where the caramelized look comes from (and a minor taste boost too). I had fig spread so used that w Calvados. The tart is unlike any I have ever made, because it has very little fruit to dough, and that glaze, making it quite rich and sweet. Other manufacturers have power management modes where it locks out max heat on some cooking zones when both ovens are heating to avoid going over 50A. Key Components of a Workout Weights Set Dumbbells: Adjustable Dumbbells: These allow you to change the weight with ease, typically through a dial or a pin system. Adjustable dumbbells save space and money by offering multiple weight options in one pair. Fixed Dumbbells: These are individual dumbbells with a specific, non-adjustable weight. They come in a variety of sizes, usually ranging from 1 lb to 100 lbs (or more). You\u2019ll find sets in increments of 5 or 10 pounds. Rubber-Coated Dumbbells: These are often preferred for home gyms because the rubber coating prevents damage to floors and reduces noise. Barbell: Standard Barbells: These usually weigh around 15-25 kg (33-55 lbs) and are used for various exercises like squats, deadlifts, and bench presses. They typically require weight plates to increase the resistance. Olympic Barbells: These are heavier, longer, and have thicker shafts, generally used for more advanced lifters and Olympic weightlifting. EZ Curl Bar: A shorter bar with a zig-zag design that is often used for exercises like bicep curls or tricep extensions. It's easier on the wrists than a straight barbell. Weight Plates: Standard Weight Plates: These are typically 1 inch in diameter and fit on standard barbells or dumbbell handles. Plates usually come in 2.5, 5, 10, 25, 35, and 45 lb increments. Bumper Plates: These are made entirely of rubber and are designed for dropping during exercises like Olympic lifts (e.g., clean and jerk, snatch). Kettlebells: Kettlebells are another form of weight, and while not typically included in a traditional \"weights set,\" they are becoming more popular in strength training routines. They\u2019re used for exercises like swings, snatches, and Turkish get-ups. They come in various weights, ranging from as light as 5-10 lbs to as heavy as 100 lbs or more. Weight Bench (Optional): A flat or adjustable weight bench can be included in some workout sets to complement exercises like bench presses, dumbbell presses, and incline/decline movements. While not always part of a basic weights set, it\u2019s a useful addition to a more comprehensive strength training routine. main_question: {"author_id": "lucillle", "author_name": "lucillle", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lucillle", "date": "2024-11-22", "text": "This may not be a general interest thread, but given the rising number of people with diabetes, it may be of interest to some. After being diagnosed with diabetes years ago I stopped eating spaghetti/pasta as it spiked my blood glucose. title: Rural Build- water filtering advice | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jessica-coughlin64", "author_name": "J C", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jessica-coughlin64", "date": "2024-11-29", "text": "We are building in a very rural area. Our well water seems to have lot of sediment, especially in certain times of the year. I\u2019m wondering what advice is out there for filtering our whole house. Is that worth it? Just filtering for drinking water? Should I avoid a fancy shower fixture and use shower head filters, maybe just for the master shower head? What about laundry? I have no expertise in this area, just want clean healthy water to drink and wash with. Thank you!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2024-12-02", "text": "Municipal water has to be regularly tested for specific list of chemicals and when they reach an actionable level, they have to be treated or mitigated. They also have a second list of chemicals that don't have defined mitigation point, but have to be tracked. When you have a private well, there's nobody but you to manage that. Do not assume your water is fine. In general there are four general areas that you need to be concerned with: 1. Biologically safe (that is to say no significant amounts of harmful bacteria or cysts) 2. Chemically safe (issues such as nitrates, heavy metals, pesticides, etc.) 3. Taste/Odor/Color - sulfur, tannins, turbidity, sediment 4. Hardness, Iron There is no one filter that will do all of that. You really do have to have your water tested by a lab before you can talk filtration at all. Then you will have things you have to deal with (1 & 2) and things you would like to deal with (3 & 4). You will have to re-test on a regular basis. Any filtering will require regular maintenance that has to be figured into things. Start by googling \"Health Dept your county well water testing\" and then testing your water. Also, what are the rules regarding testing your well before you can get building permit?", "images": []}}

title: How to make amaryllis bloom? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "central-valley", "author_name": "central_valley", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/central-valley", "date": "2024-11-30", "text": "I'm looking for authoritative advice on how to make amaryllis bloom. But I'm not sure what \"authoritative\" means in this case, because the authoritative sources I've found all say different things. For example, Holland Bulb Company says to cut the flower stalk off once the blooms have faded, and make the bulb go dormant by letting it dry out in a sunny place in late July or early August. University of Minnesota Extension says to cut the flower stalk off only when it has turned yellow, and make the bulb go dormant by letting it dry out in \"a cool, dry, dark location such as a basement or closet.\" It doesn't say when to do that, but implies \"before the first frost,\" which in northern Minnesota is mid-September, and my locale (zone 9b) is sometime between mid-December and never.
